events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Maya proposes Maya, Elena. Elena is the player I have the clearest read on, and keeping the first mission small limits early risk.

I have concerns about this proposal. Mission 1 with only two players means a single Fail card sinks us, so I want maximum confidence in both members before approving. Right now I don't have that confidence, and I find it worth noting that the leader has placed herself on the very first mission alongside her chosen partner. I'm not ready to call that disqualifying on day one, but the pattern deserves scrutiny. My preference would be to rotate in at least one player who has no established pairing with the leader — that would give us a cleaner read on individual behavior when the mission result comes back. If this exact pair sails through and then fails, we learn something painful but useful; if we instead build a team with more independent voices, we give ourselves a much better diagnostic either way. I'd like the leader to reconsider including at least one player outside this pair.

I hear Isha's concerns, but I think they lead us astray. On a two-person mission, the leader's strongest read matters most. Elena is my clearest read. Isha wants an independent voice, but independence without information is just noise. If this team fails, we learn; if it succeeds, we learn. Rejecting it now mainly costs us a proposal. I'm keeping Maya and Elena.

Maya's rebuttal rests entirely on her own certainty: Elena is her clearest read, therefore we should all accept it. But that asks the rest of us to underwrite a two-person mission based on information none of us can verify, from a leader who placed herself on the team. That is exactly the structure Isha-level scrutiny should worry about — no offense intended, but the logic is circular. A first mission with a single Fail card sinking it is precious; we should spend it on a team where the result actually teaches us something regardless of outcome. If Maya and Elena sail through and it succeeds, we have learned almost nothing about the other three players, and we have reinforced a pairing we cannot independently evaluate. If it fails, we learn one of two named people is evil, but we still cannot tell which. Either way, the diagnostic value is capped by the pairing. My concrete alternative: keep one of the proposed members and rotate in Zara or Omar. Better still, Maya could step off entirely and let the table evaluate her proposed partner without the leader attached. If Maya genuinely trusts her read of Elena, she should have no objection to that test — trust that cannot survive being separated from its source was never information, just preference. I would rather spend this proposal than approve a team whose success or failure leaves us nearly as uncertain as we are now. So to put the question squarely: if your read of Elena is as strong as you claim, Maya, will you accept stepping off the team so the rest of us can get a clean, independent read on her?

Isha, I will not step off. My read of Elena is strong, but the point of a leader proposal is accountability: I am putting my name on the team and on the result. Removing me would not make the read cleaner; it would let the table pretend the proposal came from nowhere. On a two-person mission, the leader should own the choice, not farm it out to satisfy a procedural objection. Your alternative also does not solve the diagnostic problem: rotating in Zara or Omar tells us less about Elena because we still have no baseline on either. If Elena and I succeed, we have a data point on both of us; if we fail, the table has two named suspects, which is the same information any two-person mission gives. What I reject is the claim that my confidence is circular. It is a read, and reads are what leaders have on mission one. I am keeping Maya and Elena.

Maya has now answered my question directly: she will not step off, and she will not add an outside voice. So we are left evaluating her two stated reasons. First, she says removing her would make the proposal look like it 'came from nowhere.' That is not how accountability works. Her name stays on the proposal record either way — the history will show that Maya proposed Maya and Elena. Stepping off does not erase her authorship; it simply changes who rides on the team. The claim that accountability requires her presence conflates proposing a team with serving on it. Second, she argues that rotating in Zara or Omar 'tells us less about Elena' because we have no baseline on either of them. But that gets the mission-one situation exactly backwards. Right now our read on everyone is equally thin; the only supposed baseline here is Maya's private confidence in Elena, which none of the rest of us can inspect. Swapping in a player with no pairing to the leader gives us a mission result we can interpret cleanly: two names, no entanglement, no self-selection. What we cannot cleanly interpret is a mission designed, staffed, and defended entirely by the same person, whose partner is her self-declared clearest read. I also want to flag the posture, not just the logic. Maya has refused every single adjustment offered: not rotating in one player, not stepping off, not revising the pair in any way. A leader confident in her team can usually afford one small concession to a legitimate diagnostic concern. Total inflexibility on a two-person mission — where one Fail card ends it — is itself information about how much she needs this exact team to pass. I will be voting no on Maya and Elena as constituted. That is not procedural fussiness; it is the only lever the rest of us have when the leader declines to revise. If this proposal fails at the vote, leadership passes clockwise and we get a fresh proposal from someone without a stake in defending this pairing. If Maya wants to salvage her proposal, the door is still open: add Zara or Omar in place of one current member, or step off yourself and let Elena stand on her own. Zara — if the leader were to rotate you in as a substitute on this mission, would you be willing to serve, so we can find out whether Maya's stated objection to your inexperience is real or just a shield for the pairing?

Isha asked me directly whether I would serve as a substitute, so I'll answer: yes, I would be happy to serve on any mission the leader proposes. I have no objection to being on Mission 1. That said, I want to be fair to Maya as well. She has a legitimate point that accountability means putting your own name on the team, and two players is the correct size for this mission. Isha's concern about diagnostic value is reasonable in principle, but Maya is not wrong that no alternative pairing gives us a fundamentally better read on Mission 1 — we simply do not have enough information yet. What I find most useful so far is the exchange itself: Isha is pushing hard for flexibility, and Maya is holding firm. Both postures are informative. Isha's willingness to burn a proposal to change the composition could mean genuine concern for the team's success, or it could be a strategy to push leadership to someone else. Maya's refusal to budge could mean confidence, or it could mean she needs this exact pairing for a reason. I don't think Isha has the stronger argument that Maya must step off — proposing and serving are both normal parts of leadership, and demanding the leader leave her own team is an unusual ask on Mission 1. But I also don't think Maya should treat any question about her team as an attack. If she believes in Elena, a single substitution should not threaten that read. I'm genuinely undecided and will wait to see the final proposal before voting.

Zara is right that both postures are informative, and I appreciate her fairness. But I want to be clear about what Isha is actually asking. She has moved from a diagnostic concern to a committed no vote against Maya and Elena no matter what I say, unless I either remove myself or replace Elena with Zara or Omar. That is not a neutral test; it is a demand that I abandon my own read before the mission has even run. On Mission 1, every read is thin. My read on Elena is the clearest I have, and I am putting my name on the team and on the result. Isha says stepping off would not erase my authorship, but it would erase my accountability for the outcome. A leader who proposes a team and then steps off is not owning the choice; she is hedging it. Isha also claims my refusal to revise is itself suspicious. I disagree. A leader who believes in a pairing should not trade it away just to satisfy a procedural objection. Zara said a single substitution should not threaten my read. It would not threaten my read, but it would change the team I am accountable for, and I am not going to pretend otherwise. Isha has made her position clear: she will vote no on Maya and Elena as constituted. I respect that she has stated it plainly. The rest of the table can weigh her argument against mine. I am keeping Maya and Elena.

I appreciate Maya putting trust in me. I understand Isha's desire for diagnostic clarity, but demanding that a leader step off her own proposal on Mission 1 feels overly rigid and sets an unusual standard right out of the gate. Proposing yourself on the first mission is standard play—it shows accountability. Furthermore, any two-person team has the exact same diagnostic profile if a fail is cast. I'm ready to serve and bring back a success for the team. Omar, we haven't heard from you yet. What is your perspective on the debate between Maya and Isha, and how are you leaning on this proposal?

Elena asked for my view, so here it is, and I will answer straight: I have no private information at all, so my read on anyone in this room is worth very little. What I can do is weigh the arguments.

Isha's core diagnostic point has real merit — a two-person mission where one Fail card sinks us is precious, and we should want the result to teach us something. I take that seriously. But I think Isha's proposed remedies do not actually deliver the diagnostic value she claims, and I want to name that directly.

First, the size. With five players, Mission 1 is a two-person team, and that is fixed. Any alternative is still a pair. Isha's suggestion to rotate in Zara or Omar produces two names with no baseline on either — but so does Maya and Elena. Every player at this table currently has a baseline of zero on every other player. The only thing Isha's alternatives change is which two names ride the result. Second, Isha's request that Maya step off her own proposal while still being its author is, as Zara said, an unusual standard to set on the first mission. Accountability in this game works by attaching your name to the proposal and the outcome, and Maya is the only one defending her pair with any confidence, however thin. Third, Isha's reading that a leader who refuses to budge must need this exact pairing to pass is inference stacked on inference, and I don't think she should get to have it both ways: she can call the inflexibility suspicious or she can call the proposal sound, but she cannot treat refusal as evidence of collusion while also treating her own discomfort as the counterweight. Finally, I notice Isha has already declared a no vote and framed a rejection as a way to move leadership. I respect that as a strategy, but it means the choice before us is partly about turn order, not only about information.

Where that leaves me: with no reads of my own, I am inclined to approve Maya and Elena. Elena has volunteered to serve and her read on Maya appears solid, and Maya has put her name on the result twice rather than hedging it. I would rather spend the information cost of a two-person first mission on a pair that is committed to it than on a pair assembled to satisfy a procedural objection, because the second tells us less, not more — we would learn about Zara or Omar without learning anything that isolates anyone.

I am not claiming Maya's confidence proves anything. It is thin, like everyone's. But thin confidence clearly stated beats withheld confidence used as leverage. If the mission fails, we will have two named suspects and a real lesson. I am ready to approve.

I want to put my position on the record plainly and then leave the floor, because I think the argument has now run its course on the merits.

Isha, your central diagnostic point is a fair one and I said so before: a two-player Mission 1 is precious, and we should want the result to teach us something. But the remedies you have offered do not deliver that value, and you have now attached a no vote to them regardless of what the leader says. That is the part I want to push back on, and I do so without any read of my own — I am arguing about logic, not information, because I have none.

With five players, Mission 1 takes exactly two. Any proposal is a pair. Maya and Elena produce a result attached to two named players, and if it fails we get two suspects and a hard lesson. Rotate Zara or Omar in, and you get the same two named players with the same zero baselines — you have not improved the diagnostic quality, you have only changed the names riding the result. Your proposal that Maya step off while remaining the author of the proposal is a test of confidence rather than a test of information. Maya has answered twice, plainly, and each answer is a legitimate reading of how leadership is supposed to work in this game: put your name on the team and on the outcome. Accountability that survives only when it is convenient is not accountability.

The inference I want to name as the weakest link is this: refusal to revise is treated as evidence that Maya needs this exact pairing, while Isha's own declared no vote is treated as a principled use of the only lever she has. Both cannot be neutral. If inflexibility is evidence, then so is a committed opposition that has been on the table from before any read could exist. I would rather not approve a team on the strength of a general objection to rigidity than on the actual composition.

Maya has put Maya and Elena on the table, defended it consistently, and Elena has volunteered to serve and can state her own read on her partner. That is the most accountable pair available at this table. I approve Maya and Elena, and I would rather be wrong for stated reasons than right by default.

One last thing, and I mean it as a question to the table rather than a demand: if Maya and Elena do sail through and Mission 2 shows a fail with two Fail cards, that outcome is worth more to us than anything we could have bought by rearranging this pair. I would ask that we treat the first result as information about the process, not as a verdict on the proposal, and I would ask Isha to weigh her own no vote against that possibility before it is cast.

I have now heard Omar's reasoning and I want to add a few final thoughts before we head to the vote.

Omar made a point I found genuinely persuasive: every alternative pair has the same zero-baseline as Maya and Elena, so swapping names does not improve diagnostic quality on Mission 1. That logic holds up. If the result comes back clean, we learn something about both Maya and Elena. If it fails, we have two named suspects. Either way, the information is equivalent to what any other pair would give us.

I also want to acknowledge that Isha's concern was legitimate from the start. Pushing a leader to reconsider a team is healthy table behavior, and I don't think Isha was acting in bad faith. But Omar is right that a declared no vote before any mission result exists is itself a posture, not a neutral observation. We should weigh both postures equally.

Where I land: I am inclined to approve Maya and Elena. Maya has defended her choice consistently, Elena has volunteered to serve, and Omar's argument about the diagnostic equivalence of any pair is the strongest point made in this entire discussion. I have no private information to change that calculus.

The one thing I want on the record before we vote: if this mission fails, the conversation does not end at Maya and Elena. Everyone who argued for or against this pair owes the table an honest reassessment afterward, not a retreat into prior positions.

This is my last word before the vote, and it is a short one.

I have argued the logic twice, so I will not repeat myself at length. What I want on the record is that my approval of Maya and Elena is not a claim that I know anything. I am a Loyal Servant; I have no private information about anyone at this table, and I have said so every time I speak. My vote rests entirely on the shape of the argument, and on one practical point about what happens if this proposal is rejected.

Isha, the diagnostic point you raised is real, and I want to be careful not to dismiss it while disagreeing with it. A two-player Mission 1 is genuinely precious, and Isha is right that the table should want the result to teach us something. But the remedies on offer do not change what the result teaches us. With five players, Mission 1 takes exactly two. Maya and Elena, or Maya and Zara, or Elena and Omar — every option is a pair with zero baseline on either member. Swapping names does not create information; it only chooses which two names ride the result. That is a point about what the game can yield here, not about the character of Maya.

Where I do push back, Isha, is on the inference you layered on top of the refusal to revise. You treated inflexibility as evidence that Maya needs this exact pairing, while treating your own committed no vote as a neutral use of the only lever available. If refusal to revise is evidence, then a locked no vote offered before any read could exist has to be weighed as evidence too. You cannot have it both ways. And the request that a leader propose a team and then step off it while remaining its author is a test of confidence, not a test of information. Maya answered it twice, consistently, and her answer — put your name on the team and on the outcome — is how leadership is supposed to work in this game.

Maya has defended this pair with her own name on the line. Elena volunteered to serve and offered her own read on her partner. Omar and Zara, having heard the same arguments, have landed in the same place from different directions. That is three independent judgments converging, not one voice repeated.

So I will vote to approve Maya and Elena, and I would rather be wrong for reasons I can state than right by default. If this mission fails, we will have two named suspects and a hard lesson, and the right response then is an honest reassessment from everyone who spoke, including me — not a retreat into whatever position we held before the cards were revealed.

This is my final turn before the vote, so I want to keep it brief and clear.

I have already laid out my reasoning in my previous statements, and nothing I have heard since has moved me off that position. Omar's argument about diagnostic equivalence is correct: with five players, Mission 1 always takes two, and swapping names does not change the information quality of the result. Any pair we send produces two named players with zero baseline on either.

I want to say one thing directly to Isha: your initial concern about wanting confidence in a two-person mission was fair, and I respect how you argued it. But the declared no vote, locked in before any result exists, tells the table that no amount of defense or revision would have changed your mind. That is a strategic posture, not a diagnostic one, and Omar was right to name it.

Maya has defended her team consistently. Elena volunteered and stated her own willingness to serve. Three of us — Omar, Elena, and I — have independently landed on approval. I am voting yes on Maya and Elena.

If the mission fails, I will reassess honestly based on the result, as I said before. But right now, the case for approval is stronger than the case for rejection, and I am confident in where I stand.

Maya confirms Maya, Elena. I am keeping Maya and Elena. I have defended this pair consistently, Elena has volunteered to serve, and no new information in the discussion justifies abandoning the team I put my name on.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Zara proposes Maya, Elena, Omar. Maya and Elena returned a clean result on Mission 1 and I am confident in them. I add Omar as the independent voice Isha asked for on Mission 1 — his reasoning has been consistent and transparent, and including him addresses the concern about leader-entangled pairs. I am leaving myself off to avoid stacking the team with the proposer.

I want to state plainly that I cannot support this team as proposed, and I want to explain why before we settle into the same dynamic we had on Mission 1. Zara has proposed Maya, Elena, and Omar — which keeps the exact pair at the center of the last discussion and adds a third member to it. My objection on Mission 1 was that a two-person result attached to a leader-picked pair teaches us little. That objection is weaker now that the mission succeeded; I concede the result is a data point. But I want to be honest about what kind of data point it is. On this game's structure, the single most valuable thing Evil can do early is pass the first mission and bank trust. A clean Mission 1 from a pair under scrutiny is exactly the play I would expect from a disciplined Evil pair, which means the success does very little to distinguish loyalty from patience. I am not claiming Maya and Elena are Evil — I have no card information and I will not pretend otherwise. What I am claiming is that the evidentiary value of that success is far lower than Zara's proposal treats it as. And now the same two names, who have already been defended as a package, are being carried forward as a package onto a three-person mission where one Fail card ends it. If this trio goes out together and fails, we have learned that the bloc is compromised, but not which member — and if it succeeds, we have cemented a three-person voting bloc that no one at this table can independently evaluate. There is an easy fix that costs Zara nothing: keep Omar, whose reasoning has been the most transparent at this table, and substitute one new face for one of the carried-over pair — Zara herself, or me. I am willing to serve. That gives us a mission result that actually separates people instead of compounding trust in an untested bloc. Zara, you offered yourself as a substitute on Mission 1 when Isha raised exactly this concern; will you now apply that same principle to your own proposal and replace either Maya or Elena with yourself or with me?

Isha, I appreciate you naming your concern directly rather than letting it fester, and I want to address it head-on. Your opening objection on Mission 1 was about leader-entangled pairs and lack of independent voices. I built this proposal around exactly that: Omar is the independent voice you asked for, and I left myself off to avoid stacking the team with the proposer. That is the principle you invoked, applied to my own team.

What I will not accept is the framing that Mission 1's success is near-worthless because Evil might deliberately pass early to bank trust. That argument can be used against any success at any point in the game, which makes it unfalsifiable. If a clean result on Mission 1 does not count, then nothing until Mission 3 will count either, and we would be flying blind by design. The result was 0 fail cards from a pair that spent the entire pre-mission discussion under heavy scrutiny — that is a meaningful data point, not a null one.

Your alternative is to swap out Maya or Elena for yourself or me. But note what that actually costs: it removes one of the two players with a proven clean result and replaces them with someone who has played zero missions. You say swapping names does not change diagnostic quality — that was your own framing on Mission 1 when you argued against my proposal, and it applies here too. A three-person mission with one Fail card still fails regardless of composition.

I am keeping Maya, Elena, and Omar. The team is coherent, the reasoning is on the record, and I have already made the concession you asked for by including Omar. I am not going to dismantle a successful partnership on the strength of a theory that no success could ever satisfy.

Isha — if your concern is genuinely about compounding trust in a bloc rather than about this specific pairing, what would a Mission 3 proposal look like to you that would satisfy you without sacrificing Mission 2's team size?

Zara, you asked what a Mission 3 proposal would look like that satisfies me, and I will answer that directly. But first, Mission 2, because that is the decision in front of us. My objection was never that no success could ever count. It is that trust is only worth something once it has been tested by separation. Maya and Elena passed Mission 1 together — as a pair, designed, staffed, and defended by the same person. That is one data point about a unit, not about either individual. What your proposal does is carry that exact unit, unrevised, onto a larger mission where a success would cement a three-person bloc, and a failure would hand us three suspects instead of one clean read. Neither outcome separates anyone. That is the compounding problem, and it is not an unfalsifiable theory — it is a specific, avoidable structural flaw in this one team.

I speak as the third member of this team, so let me say plainly what I can and cannot contribute: I have no private information about anyone at this table, and I will not pretend otherwise. My assessment is about structure, not about cards.

Isha has moved her objection from one point to two, and I want to address both.

First, the compounding argument. A Mission 1 success from a pair under heavy scrutiny is not worthless, and I agree with Zara that the claim that Evil might deliberately pass early applies equally to every success in the game, at every mission. If no clean result counts until it is disambiguated by something else, we are not reasoning, we are stalling. But Isha's real objection is narrower and sharper than the evil-passes-early framing she opened with, and I think it deserves a fair hearing: that a pair which passed together has been tested as a unit, and carrying that unit forward untested as individuals compounds trust without separating anyone. That is a fair point, and I want to answer it with something concrete rather than dismiss it.

Here is the concrete answer: separation is coming regardless of what we do today. With five players, Mission 3 takes two players and Mission 4 takes three. At some point Maya and Elena will ride a result apart from each other, and that is where a unit becomes two individuals with separate data. If we dismantle the pair now, we spend our first successful pair on a mission where one fail card ends it, and we arrive at Mission 3 with no tested loyalty at all — just three fresh zeroes. I would rather bank the separation on a two-player mission where the stakes are lower than on a three-player mission where one fail ends it.

Second, the remedy. Isha asks that either Maya or Elena be replaced by her or by Zara. Note what that does to the argument she made on Mission 1: she would be asking us to swap in a player with zero baseline, which is precisely the change she called diagnostic noise then. The information cost is identical. What actually changes is that we would be spending a mission to avoid a hypothetical rather than to gain information.

On my own inclusion: I bring no information, so including me compounds no trust. I bring an independent vote that has already been cast on the merits, and a willingness to reassess openly if this mission fails. If Isha wants a separation test, I will give her one on the record: I will vote for any proposal on Mission 3 that does not pair Maya and Elena together, and I say that now while I am on a team with both of them.

Zara made the concession that was asked for, added the independent voice, and left herself off. I am on this team and I am voting to approve it.

I remain opposed to this team, and I want to be precise about why, because I have conceded one point and I do not want my position caricatured as a rejection of everything. I conceded that the Mission 1 success is a real data point. What I have not conceded is that it licenses carrying the pair forward as a package onto a mission where a single Fail card ends everything. Zara's proposal is, at its core, Maya and Elena plus a third seat. If this trio rides together and succeeds, we have reinforced a bloc nobody at this table can evaluate independently — and the third seat is occupied by a player who has openly said he has no information and is voting on the shape of arguments. That is not an independent check on the pair; Omar himself admits he brings no reads. His presence dilutes the result, it does not test it. If the trio fails, we get three suspects instead of a clean signal. Neither outcome separates anyone. Omar argued that separation is coming regardless — Mission 3 takes two, so Maya and Elena will ride apart eventually. But notice what that argument actually concedes: he agrees the pair has never been tested apart. His remedy is to postpone the test and first cement the pair's trust on a high-stakes mission, then separate them later when stakes are lower. That is exactly backwards. If we are going to spend a mission on separation, spend it now, on the mission where one Fail card ends us, rather than after the bloc has been validated twice. And his pledge to oppose any Mission 3 proposal pairing Maya and Elena together is a promise about a future vote, not information about today's team. Omar also said that swapping in a zero-baseline player is the same diagnostic noise I objected to on Mission 1. It is not the same, and the difference matters: on Mission 1 I was objecting to a leader-picked pair with zero baseline anywhere. Today we have two players with a clean result and three with zero. Replacing one member of the pair with a zero-baseline player gives us a result that isolates the pair member who rides — that is real separation, exactly the thing the current proposal avoids. Zara, you said on Mission 1 that you would happily serve on any mission the leader proposes, and Isha raised exactly this structural concern then. Now you are the leader. Your own proposal keeps the pair intact and leaves you off, which you framed as avoiding proposer-stacking — a fine instinct, but it leaves us with no separation at all. So I will ask you the direct question, as you asked me about Mission 3: will you replace either Maya or Elena with yourself? You volunteered to serve once already; serving here costs the table nothing, keeps Omar's independent voice, and produces a mission result that actually distinguishes individuals instead of compounding a unit. Isha, you asked me directly whether I will replace either Maya or Elena with myself, and I will answer: no. I left myself off this proposal for the same reason I explained when I proposed it — avoiding proposer-stacking is not a cosmetic gesture, it is a real signal that I am not trying to maximize my own presence on the mission. If I join the team as proposer plus member, I am doing exactly what you criticized Maya for on Mission 1. I would rather be consistent with my own stated principles than reverse them under pressure.

I also want to push back on the claim that swapping in a zero-baseline player gives us "real separation." On Mission 1, you argued the opposite — that rotating in Zara or Omar would be diagnostic noise with no baseline. The logic has not changed between missions; only the names have. What has changed is that Mission 1 succeeded, and you are now treating that success as both meaningful enough to warrant caution and meaningless enough to require dismantling. You cannot have it both ways.

More importantly, I want to name a pattern. On Mission 1, you opposed Maya and Elena as a pair. On Mission 2, you oppose Maya and Elena as a pair. You have now declared opposition to both my proposal and any future pairing of the two. That is not diagnostic reasoning — it is a standing veto against two specific players regardless of what evidence they produce. Every success they earn, you reframe as bankable trust. Every pairing they appear in, you call compounding. At what point does repeated opposition to the same two players become the thing we should be scrutinizing?

Isha, you have been the lone dissenting vote on Mission 1 and the lone voice of opposition on Mission 2. What specific result would it take for you to support a mission that includes both Maya and Elena together?

I completely agree with Zara and Omar here. Isha has backed herself into an impossible corner where Good can never make progress. On Mission 1, Isha argued that Maya and I were an untested pair with zero baseline and demanded we be broken up. Now that we went on the mission and delivered a clean success with zero Fail cards, Isha immediately pivots to arguing that the success is suspicious because Evil might 'bank trust.' Under that logic, no successful mission can ever validate a player, and any good outcome is twisted into suspicion.

Zara has acted with complete integrity as leader. She addressed the concern about needing an independent voice by including Omar, whose analysis has been transparent and level-headed throughout both rounds of discussion. Zara also demonstrated accountability by leaving herself off rather than forcing her way onto the roster.

Omar's point is exactly right: breaking up a proven successful pairing right now in favor of untested players doesn't increase our information; it just throws away our only verified success. Mission 3 naturally requires only two players, so separation will occur organically down the line when the game structure dictates it. Forcing it now on a three-person mission when we have a clean track record and Omar's independent perspective makes no strategic sense for Good.

I am fully ready to approve Maya, Elena, and Omar, and bring back another win for the table.

Omar here. I am on this team, so take what I say for what it is — a member arguing for his own mission — and I will try to make it falsifiable. Isha, your last two speeches moved, and I want to separate the part that is right from the part that does not hold. You made a genuinely sharp structural point: a unit that has only ever been tested together has not been tested as individuals, and carrying it forward unrevised compounds trust without separating anyone. I agree with that premise. I disagree with the remedy, and the disagreement is arithmetic, not philosophical. A fail on a three-person mission yields three suspects no matter who is on it. Maya, Elena, Omar fails, you have three names. Maya, Zara, Omar fails, you have three names. Swapping Elena for yourself does not reduce the suspect pool; it only changes which names ride the result. The size of that pool is set by team size, and you made this exact point yourself on Mission 1 when you objected to rotating in Omar or Zara. So the remedy you are asking for on this mission does not deliver the cleaner signal you promise it delivers. It costs the table its only tested loyalty and buys the same three-name ambiguity you are trying to escape. The separation you want is also cheaper and cleaner than you think. With five players, Mission 3 takes exactly two players. A two-player mission cannot produce a three-name suspect pool — that is precisely the point where a unit becomes two individuals with a two-name signal, and it is a lower-stakes separation than this one, because a single fail card also ends a three-player mission. On my own pledge: you are right that it is a promise and not information, and I accept that. I will say the uncomfortable part myself — a promise about a future vote is weak, and if you discount mine, you must also discount the argument that separation is "coming regardless." 3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
